claim: More than half of long-term brain tumor survivors develop irreversible cognitive decline that severely affects their quality of life.
source: More than half of long-term brain tumor survivors develop irreversible cognitive decline that severely affect their quality of life.
evidence: This is a general statement about clinical outcomes in brain tumor survivors, drawing from established medical knowledge.

claim: There is no pre-clinical model that allows long-term assessment of cognition in brain tumor research.
source: However, there is no pre-clinical model that allows long-term assessment of cognition, and there is no treatment which ameliorates cognitive deficits in patients.
evidence: This statement reflects the gap in existing research models, based on knowledge of the field.

claim: There is no treatment which ameliorates cognitive deficits in brain tumor patients.
source: However, there is no pre-clinical model that allows long-term assessment of cognition, and there is no treatment which ameliorates cognitive deficits in patients.
evidence: This reflects current clinical knowledge about treatment limitations.

claim: A novel glioma mouse model offers manageable tumor growth and reliable assessment of cognitive functions in a post-treatment manner.
source: Here, we report a novel glioma mouse model that offers manageable tumor growth and reliable assessment of cognitive functions in a post-treatment manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript showing survival curves, BLI imaging, and cognitive testing results.

claim: Fractionated whole-brain irradiation (fWBI), but not tumor growth, results in memory deficits.
source: Using this model, we found that fractionated whole-brain irradiation (fWBI), but not tumor growth, results in memory deficits.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Novel Object Recognition tests shown in Figure 2.

claim: Transient inhibition of CSF-1R during fWBI prolongs survival of glioma-bearing mice.
source: Transient inhibition of CSF-1R during fWBI prolongs survival of glioma-bearing mice and fully prevents fWBI-induced memory deficits.
evidence: This is supported by survival curve data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: Transient inhibition of CSF-1R during fWBI fully prevents fWBI-induced memory deficits.
source: Transient inhibition of CSF-1R during fWBI prolongs survival of glioma-bearing mice and fully prevents fWBI-induced memory deficits.
evidence: This is supported by Novel Object Recognition test data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: CSF-1R inhibition during radiotherapy can be explored as an approach to improve both survival and cognitive outcomes in patients who will receive fWBI.
source: This result suggests that CSF-1R inhibition during radiotherapy can be explored as an approach to improve both survival and cognitive outcomes in patients who will receive fWBI.
evidence: This is a speculative translational inference based on the experimental results.

claim: Cognitive deficits are seen in more than half of patients who received fractionated whole brain irradiation (fWBI).
source: However, cognitive deficits are still seen in more than half of the patients who received fractionated whole brain irradiation (fWBI) (Meyers and Brown, 2006; Greene-Schloesser and Robbins, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Approximately 100,000 brain tumor patients survive long enough to experience radiation-induced cognitive deficits in the US alone each year.
source: Despite an overall poor longterm outcome, each year approximately 100,000 brain tumor patients survive long enough to experience radiation-induced cognitive deficits in the US alone (Greene-Schloesser and Robbins, 2012).
evidence: This epidemiological claim is supported by a citation.

claim: The quality of life of long-term brain tumor survivors is severely affected by impairments in cognitive function.
source: The quality of life of these long-term survivors is severely affected by the impairments in cognitive function.
evidence: This reflects established clinical knowledge about patient outcomes.

claim: There is no treatment to ameliorate radiation-induced cognitive deficits.
source: Unfortunately, there is no treatment to ameliorate these adverse effects.
evidence: This reflects current clinical knowledge.

claim: Single fraction of WBI induces changes in neurogenesis and neuronal structures.
source: Previous studies have shown that single fraction of WBI induces a number of deleterious effects, including changes in neurogenesis and neuronal structures, activation of microglia and astrocytes, and accumulation of peripheral immune cells in the central nervous system (CNS) (Monje et al., 2002; Mizumatsu et al., 2003; Monje and Palmer, 2003; Monje et al., 2007; Rola et al., 2007; Monje, 2008; Fike et al., 2009; Morganti et al., 2014; Feng et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Single fraction of WBI induces activation of microglia and astrocytes.
source: Previous studies have shown that single fraction of WBI induces a number of deleterious effects, including changes in neurogenesis and neuronal structures, activation of microglia and astrocytes, and accumulation of peripheral immune cells in the central nervous system (CNS) (Monje et al., 2002; Mizumatsu et al., 2003; Monje and Palmer, 2003; Monje et al., 2007; Rola et al., 2007; Monje, 2008; Fike et al., 2009; Morganti et al., 2014; Feng et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Single fraction of WBI induces accumulation of peripheral immune cells in the central nervous system (CNS).
source: Previous studies have shown that single fraction of WBI induces a number of deleterious effects, including changes in neurogenesis and neuronal structures, activation of microglia and astrocytes, and accumulation of peripheral immune cells in the central nervous system (CNS) (Monje et al., 2002; Mizumatsu et al., 2003; Monje and Palmer, 2003; Monje et al., 2007; Rola et al., 2007; Monje, 2008; Fike et al., 2009; Morganti et al., 2014; Feng et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: fWBI, simulating a clinical treatment schedule, recapitulates the findings observed with a single fraction of radiation.
source: We have previously demonstrated that fWBI, simulating a clinical treatment schedule, recapitulates the findings observed with a single fraction of radiation.
evidence: This refers to previous work by the authors, implying citation to their own research.

claim: The activation of inflammatory pathways is a critical factor in the initiation of radiation-induced brain injury.
source: From a mechanistic perspective, there is considerable evidence that the activation of inflammatory pathways is a critical factor in the initiation of radiation-induced brain injury (Morganti et al., 2014; Acharya et al., 2016; Feng et al., 2016; Moravan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Colony-Stimulating Factor 1 (CSF-1) is a cytokine involved in the recruitment/activation of myeloid cell precursors to areas of injury.
source: The Colony-Stimulating Factor 1 (CSF-1) is a cytokine involved in the recruitment/activation of myeloid cell precursors to areas of injury.
evidence: This reflects established biological knowledge about CSF-1 function.

claim: Using a CSF-1 receptor (CSF-1R) inhibitor during fWBI resulted in a transient depletion of microglia.
source: We have shown that using a CSF-1 receptor (CSF-1R) inhibitor during fWBI resulted in a transient depletion of microglia, a lower number of activated microglia, and lower numbers of inflammatory monocyte accumulating in the CNS.
evidence: This refers to previous work by the authors.

claim: Using a CSF-1R inhibitor during fWBI resulted in a lower number of activated microglia.
source: We have shown that using a CSF-1 receptor (CSF-1R) inhibitor during fWBI resulted in a transient depletion of microglia, a lower number of activated microglia, and lower numbers of inflammatory monocyte accumulating in the CNS.
evidence: This refers to previous work by the authors.

claim: Using a CSF-1R inhibitor during fWBI resulted in lower numbers of inflammatory monocytes accumulating in the CNS.
source: We have shown that using a CSF-1 receptor (CSF-1R) inhibitor during fWBI resulted in a transient depletion of microglia, a lower number of activated microglia, and lower numbers of inflammatory monocyte accumulating in the CNS.
evidence: This refers to previous work by the authors.

claim: Use of a CSF-1R inhibitor fully prevented radiation-induced long term cognitive impairments in mice.
source: More importantly, use of a CSF-1R inhibitor fully prevented radiation-induced long term cognitive impairments in mice (Acharya et al., 2016; Feng et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Activated microglia and peripherally-derived monocytes are often recruited secondary to initiation and growth of brain tumors (gliomas in particular).
source: However, since activated microglia and peripherally-derived monocytes are often recruited secondary to initiation and growth of brain tumors (gliomas in particular), it is not clear whether radiation-induced cognitive changes are modified or attenuated in tumor-bearing animals (Pyonteck et al., 2013; Stafford et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: It is not clear whether radiation-induced cognitive changes are modified or attenuated in tumor-bearing animals.
source: However, since activated microglia and peripherally-derived monocytes are often recruited secondary to initiation and growth of brain tumors (gliomas in particular), it is not clear whether radiation-induced cognitive changes are modified or attenuated in tumor-bearing animals (Pyonteck et al., 2013; Stafford et al., 2016).
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge based on inference from existing literature.

claim: Cognitive studies in glioma animal models following radiation treatment have not been previously reported.
source: Cognitive studies in glioma animal models following radiation treatment have not been previously reported.
evidence: This reflects knowledge of the existing literature.

claim: The primary reason cognitive studies have not been done in glioma models is the technical challenge of producing a glioma-bearing animal that survives sufficiently long enough for cognitive assessment.
source: The primary reason is the technical challenge of producing a glioma-bearing animal that survives sufficiently long enough for cognitive assessment.
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge of experimental limitations.

claim: Low grade glioma models tend to have long, and unpredictable tumor onset with variable growth rates.
source: Low grade glioma models tend to have long, and unpredictable tumor onset with variable growth rates, while high grade glioma models tend to be aggressive with an insufficient time window to permit assays of cognitive function (Chen et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and reflects knowledge of glioma models.

claim: High grade glioma models tend to be aggressive with an insufficient time window to permit assays of cognitive function.
source: Low grade glioma models tend to have long, and unpredictable tumor onset with variable growth rates, while high grade glioma models tend to be aggressive with an insufficient time window to permit assays of cognitive function (Chen et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and reflects knowledge of glioma models.

claim: Most models using human xenografted tumors require an immunodeficient host, which would severely limit the ability to study the role of the immune system in cognitive function.
source: Most models using human xenografted tumors require an immunodeficient host, which would severely limit the ability to study the role of the immune system in cognitive function.
evidence: This reflects knowledge of xenograft model limitations and inference about their impact on immune studies.

claim: Transgenic mouse models have an inherent inconsistency in tumor development and progression which would preclude the ability to perform cognitive testing at predictable times following radiation treatment.
source: Finally, transgenic mouse models have an inherent inconsistency in tumor development and progression which would preclude the ability to perform cognitive testing at predictable times following radiation treatment.
evidence: This reflects knowledge of transgenic model limitations and inference about their impact on cognitive testing.

claim: fWBI or CSF-1R treatment alone significantly prolonged the survival of animals after tumor implantation.
source: We found that fWBI or CSF-1R treatment alone significantly prolonged the survival of animals after tumor implantation.
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Memory deficits were detected only in mice received fWBI but not in non-irradiated tumor bearing mice.
source: However, strikingly, memory deficits were detected only in mice received fWBI but not in non-irradiated tumor bearing mice.
evidence: This is supported by Novel Object Recognition test data shown in Figure 2.

claim: CSF-1R inhibitor treatment was able to prevent fWBI-induced memory loss in glioma bearing animals.
source: Finally, we demonstrated that CSF-1R inhibitor treatment was able to prevent fWBI-induced memory loss in glioma bearing animals.
evidence: This is supported by Novel Object Recognition test data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: GL261-DTR cells were created by stably transfecting Diphtheria Toxin Receptor (DTR) into GL261-luc cell line.
source: To create a growth-manageable glioma model we stably transfected Diphtheria Toxin Receptor (DTR) into GL261-luc cell line (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used to create the model, with supporting image data.

claim: GL261-DTR cells formed tumors indistinguishable from non-DTR expression GL261 cells when injected into the mouse brain.
source: When injected into the mouse brain, the GL261-DTR cells formed tumors indistinguishable from non-DTR expression GL261 cells (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is stated but the supporting data is not shown in the manuscript.

claim: Six doses of DT injection at 1 µg/mouse/daily significantly prolonged the survival of tumor bearing mice.
source: Six doses of DT injection at 1 µg/mouse/daily significantly prolonged the survival of tumor bearing mice (Figure 1A), and resulted in delayed increase of bioluminescence imaging (BLI) signals from tumor cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by survival curve data in Figure 1A.

claim: Six doses of DT injection at 1 µg/mouse/daily resulted in delayed increase of bioluminescence imaging (BLI) signals from tumor cells.
source: Six doses of DT injection at 1 µg/mouse/daily significantly prolonged the survival of tumor bearing mice (Figure 1A), and resulted in delayed increase of bioluminescence imaging (BLI) signals from tumor cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by BLI data in Figure 1B.

claim: Survival was further improved when DT treatment was combined with fWBI.
source: Survival was further improved when DT treatment was combined with fWBI (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by survival curve data in Figure 1A.

claim: Combined DT and fWBI treatment resulted in a more dramatic decrease in BLI signals from tumor cells.
source: This regimen (DT treatment and fWBI) resulted in a more dramatic decrease in BLI signals from tumor cells; and a new round of DT treatment (1 µg/mouse every other day) slowed tumor growth in four of the five mice with recurrent tumors (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by BLI data in Figure 1C.

claim: A new round of DT treatment (1 µg/mouse every other day) slowed tumor growth in four of the five mice with recurrent tumors.
source: This regimen (DT treatment and fWBI) resulted in a more dramatic decrease in BLI signals from tumor cells; and a new round of DT treatment (1 µg/mouse every other day) slowed tumor growth in four of the five mice with recurrent tumors (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by BLI data in Figure 1C.

claim: The GL261-DTR glioma model has a predictable and manageable pattern of tumor growth in vivo, which allows delayed cognitive assessments.
source: These results demonstrate that the GL261-DTR glioma model has a predictable and manageable pattern of tumor growth in vivo, which allows delayed cognitive assessments.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing controlled tumor growth and extended survival.

claim: The median survival of DT treated tumor bearing mice was extended to 31 days.
source: The medium survival of DT treated tumor bearing mice was extended to 31 days (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by survival curve data in Figure 1A.

claim: DT treatment was able to temporarily inhibit tumor growth, as evidenced by reduced BLI signals compared to the non-treated group.
source: DT treatment was able to temporarily inhibit tumor growth, as evidenced by reduced BLI signals compared to the non-treated group (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by BLI data in Figure 1B.

claim: No side effects beside moderate weight loss (<10%) were observed in DT treated mice.
source: No side effects beside moderate weight loss (<10%, data not shown) were observed in DT treated mice.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiment, though the data is not shown.

claim: In the DT + fWBI group, higher efficacy of tumor growth inhibition was achieved.
source: In the DT + fWBI group, higher efficacy of tumor growth inhibition was achieved (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by BLI data in Figure 1C.

claim: The DT + fWBI paradigm extended the median survival to 46 days, more than 4 weeks after the completion of fWBI.
source: This paradigm further extended the medium survival to 46 days, more than 4 weeks after the completion of fWBI (Figure 1A), thus permitting assessment of cognitive function in these mice at a timepoint that matches our previously reported results using tumor-free models (Belarbi et al., 2013; Feng et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by survival curve data in Figure 1A and references to previous work.

claim: No recognition memory deficits were detected in GL261-DTR bearing mice between day 13 and day 16 after tumor implantation despite tumors in their brains.
source: Strikingly, no recognition memory deficits were detected in these mice despite of tumors in their brains (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by Novel Object Recognition test data in Figure 2A.

claim: A previous report demonstrated hippocampal dysfunction in mice with subcutaneous sarcoma.
source: A previous report demonstrated hippocampal dysfunction in mice with subcutaneous sarcoma (Yang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Sarcoma bearing mice have increased plasma and hippocampal IL-6 concentrations compared to tumor-free animals.
source: In their study, Yang et al demonstrated that there is increased plasma and hippocampal IL-6 concentrations in sarcoma bearing mice compared to tumor-free animals, as well as elevated plasma corticosterone levels.
evidence: This claim is based on a cited study by Yang et al.

claim: Sarcoma bearing mice have elevated plasma corticosterone levels.
source: In their study, Yang et al demonstrated that there is increased plasma and hippocampal IL-6 concentrations in sarcoma bearing mice compared to tumor-free animals, as well as elevated plasma corticosterone levels.
evidence: This claim is based on a cited study by Yang et al.

claim: Changes in immune and endocrine systems induced neuroinflammation and were responsible for cognitive deficits in sarcoma bearing mice.
source: These changes in immune and endocrine systems induced neuroinflammation and were responsible for the observed cognitive deficits.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited Yang et al. study.

claim: GBM growth can lead to increased plasma IL-6 levels.
source: It has been reported that GBM growth can lead to increased plasma IL-6 levels (Lamano et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: It is not known whether hippocampal IL-6 levels are increased with GBM growing in the right frontal cortex.
source: However, it is not known whether hippocampal IL-6 levels are also increased with GBM growing in the right frontal cortex.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge.

claim: Memory deficits are seen in brain tumor patients prior to treatments, but only when brain regions involved in memory functions are directly disrupted by glioma growth.
source: It is worth noting that memory deficits are seen in brain tumor patients prior to treatments, but only when brain regions involved in memory functions are directly disrupted by glioma growth (van Kessel et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: In the GL261-DTR glioma model, tumor growth in the right frontal cortex does not affect recognition memory.
source: Concordantly, in our GL261-DTR glioma model, the tumor growth in the right frontal cortex does not affect recognition memory.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data from Figure 2A and comparison with clinical observations.

claim: CSF-1R is expressed in microglia, peripheral monocytes/macrophages and tumor associated macrophages.
source: CSF-1R is expressed in microglia, peripheral monocytes/macrophages and tumor associated macrophages.
evidence: This reflects established biological knowledge about CSF-1R expression.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of CSF-1R has shown advantages in preventing cranial irradiation-induced cognitive deficits in tumor-free models.
source: Pharmacological inhibition of CSF-1R has shown advantages in preventing cranial irradiation-induced cognitive deficits in tumor-free models (Acharya et al., 2016; Feng et al., 2016), prolonging survival in glioma-bearing mice (Pyonteck et al., 2013), and delaying the recurrence of glioma after radiotherapy (Stafford et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of CSF-1R prolongs survival in glioma-bearing mice.
source: Pharmacological inhibition of CSF-1R has shown advantages in preventing cranial irradiation-induced cognitive deficits in tumor-free models (Acharya et al., 2016; Feng et al., 2016), prolonging survival in glioma-bearing mice (Pyonteck et al., 2013), and delaying the recurrence of glioma after radiotherapy (Stafford et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of CSF-1R delays the recurrence of glioma after radiotherapy.
source: Pharmacological inhibition of CSF-1R has shown advantages in preventing cranial irradiation-induced cognitive deficits in tumor-free models (Acharya et al., 2016; Feng et al., 2016), prolonging survival in glioma-bearing mice (Pyonteck et al., 2013), and delaying the recurrence of glioma after radiotherapy (Stafford et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Treatment with fWBI alone was able to improve survival after tumor implantation, but not to the extent of DT treatment alone.
source: Treatment with fWBI alone was able to improve survival after tumor implantation, but not to the extent of DT treatment alone, while combined DT and fWBI treatment resulted in better survival than either single treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by survival curve data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Combined DT and fWBI treatment resulted in better survival than either single treatment.
source: Treatment with fWBI alone was able to improve survival after tumor implantation, but not to the extent of DT treatment alone, while combined DT and fWBI treatment resulted in better survival than either single treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by survival curve data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CSF-1R inhibitor treatment alone did not prolong survival of tumor bearing mice.
source: CSF-1R inhibitor treatment alone did not prolong survival of tumor bearing mice.
evidence: This is supported by survival data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: With combined CSF-1R inhibitor and fWBI treatments, survival was significantly improved compared to inhibitor alone, but was not significantly different from fWBI alone.
source: With combined CSF-1R inhibitor and fWBI treatments, survival was significantly improved compared to inhibitor alone, but was not significantly different from fWBI alone (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by survival data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: DT, but not CSF-1R inhibitor, acted as a radiosensitizer in the GL261-DTR model.
source: Therefore, DT, but not CSF-1R inhibitor, acted as a radiosensitizer in our GL261-DTR model, which allowed us to extend survival of tumor bearing mice long enough for cognitive assessment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the survival data comparing different treatment combinations.

claim: DT +fWBI treatment significantly improved survival in the GL261-DTR model.
source: We found that DT +fWBI or DT +CSF-1R inhibitor treatment significantly improved survival in the GL261-DTR model (Figure 2B, blue and green lines).
evidence: This is supported by survival curve data in Figure 2B.

claim: DT +CSF-1R inhibitor treatment significantly improved survival in the GL261-DTR model.
source: We found that DT +fWBI or DT +CSF-1R inhibitor treatment significantly improved survival in the GL261-DTR model (Figure 2B, blue and green lines).
evidence: This is supported by survival curve data in Figure 2B.

claim: Combined DT, CSF-1R inhibitor and fWBI treatment did not improve survival time of tumor bearing mice.
source: Combined DT, CSF-1R inhibitor and fWBI treatment did not improve survival time of tumor bearing mice (Figure 2B, black line).
evidence: This is supported by survival curve data in Figure 2B.

claim: CSF-1R inhibitor treatment was able to prevent memory deficits induced by fWBI in tumor bearing mice.
source: Most importantly, CSF-1R inhibitor treatment was able to prevent memory deficits induced by fWBI in tumor bearing mice (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by Novel Object Recognition test data in Figure 2C.

claim: There was no difference in velocity during the test trials among treatment groups.
source: There was no difference in velocity or time spent in the center of arena (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D) during the test trials, suggesting that no motor dysfunction or increase of anxiety was caused by tumor growth or treatments at the time of Novel Object Recognition (NOR) test.
evidence: This is supported by Open Field test data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There was no difference in time spent in the center of arena during the test trials among treatment groups.
source: There was no difference in velocity or time spent in the center of arena (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D) during the test trials, suggesting that no motor dysfunction or increase of anxiety was caused by tumor growth or treatments at the time of Novel Object Recognition (NOR) test.
evidence: This is supported by Open Field test data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: No motor dysfunction was caused by tumor growth or treatments at the time of Novel Object Recognition test.
source: There was no difference in velocity or time spent in the center of arena (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D) during the test trials, suggesting that no motor dysfunction or increase of anxiety was caused by tumor growth or treatments at the time of Novel Object Recognition (NOR) test.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Open Field test data.

claim: No increase of anxiety was caused by tumor growth or treatments at the time of Novel Object Recognition test.
source: There was no difference in velocity or time spent in the center of arena (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D) during the test trials, suggesting that no motor dysfunction or increase of anxiety was caused by tumor growth or treatments at the time of Novel Object Recognition (NOR) test.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Open Field test data.

claim: This is the first demonstration that tumor-bearing mice are susceptible to fWBI-induced memory deficits.
source: These results demonstrate for the first time that tumor-bearing mice are susceptible to fWBI-induced memory deficits, and temporary inhibition of CSF-1R during fWBI is sufficient to prevent radiation-induced deficits.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data and knowledge of the literature.

claim: Temporary inhibition of CSF-1R during fWBI is sufficient to prevent radiation-induced cognitive deficits in tumor-bearing mice.
source: These results demonstrate for the first time that tumor-bearing mice are susceptible to fWBI-induced memory deficits, and temporary inhibition of CSF-1R during fWBI is sufficient to prevent radiation-induced deficits.
evidence: This is supported by the Novel Object Recognition test data in Figure 2C.

claim: Animals in the tumor +DT group showed no recognition memory deficits.
source: Similar to the tumor-only group, animals in the tumor +DT group also showed no recognition memory deficits (Figure 2C), further demonstrating that glioma growth does not affect recognition memory.
evidence: This is supported by Novel Object Recognition test data in Figure 2C.

claim: Glioma growth does not affect recognition memory.
source: Similar to the tumor-only group, animals in the tumor +DT group also showed no recognition memory deficits (Figure 2C), further demonstrating that glioma growth does not affect recognition memory.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Novel Object Recognition test data from tumor-bearing mice without radiation.

claim: Increased CD11b expression level has been used as an indicator of microglia activation during CNS inflammation.
source: Increased CD11b expression level has been used as an indicator of microglia activation during CNS inflammation (Hoogland et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: There was no significant change in microglial CD11b MFI after irradiation compared to non-irradiated mice.
source: We found no significant change in microglial CD11b MFI after irradiation compared to non-irradiated mice.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3A.

claim: CSF-1R inhibitor treatment resulted in significant reduction of CD11b MFI compared to untreated groups.
source: Conversely, CSF-1R inhibitor treatment resulted in significant reduction of CD11b MFI compared to untreated groups (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3A.

claim: No morphological changes of hippocampal microglia were induced by irradiation.
source: Immunofluorescent staining for Iba1, a macrophage specific marker, revealed that no morphological changes of hippocampal microglia were induced by irradiation (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescent staining images in Figure 3D.

claim: There was a trend for an increase in the Iba1 stained area in the hippocampus after irradiation, which was reversed by CSF-1R inhibitor treatment.
source: However, there was a trend for an increase in the Iba1 stained area in the hippocampus, which was reveresed by CSF-1R inhibitor treatment (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data in Figure 3B.

claim: Radiation induced a significant increase in activated microglia (CD68+ cells).
source: Co-staining for microglia activation marker CD68 suggest that radiation induced a significant increase in activated microglia, which was significantly reduced in animals treated with CSF-1R inhibitor (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescent staining and quantification data in Figure 3C.

claim: Activated microglia induced by radiation were significantly reduced in animals treated with CSF-1R inhibitor.
source: Co-staining for microglia activation marker CD68 suggest that radiation induced a significant increase in activated microglia, which was significantly reduced in animals treated with CSF-1R inhibitor (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescent staining and quantification data in Figure 3C.

claim: Treatment with CSF-1R inhibitor reduced microglial reactivity in the hippocampus.
source: Consistent with the CD11b results, the immunohistochemistry data suggest that treatment with CSF-1R inhibitor reduced microglial reactivity in the hippocampus.
evidence: This is an inference based on the immunohistochemistry data in Figure 3.

claim: Cranial irradiation induces morphological changes that correlate with microglia activation, including increased Iba1+ and CD68+ cell numbers and staining coverage.
source: Previous reports have demonstrated that cranial irradiation induces morphological changes that correlate with microglia activation, including increased Iba1 +and CD68+cell numbers and staining coverage (Chiang et al., 1993; Acharya et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Cranial irradiation induced microglia activation can be prevented by CSF-1R inhibitor mediated depletion in the presence of brain tumors.
source: Taken together with the present results, this work confirmed that cranial irradiation induced microglia activation can be prevented by CSF-1R inhibitor mediated depletion in the presence of brain tumors.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data and comparison with previous literature.

claim: fWBI-induced cognitive deficits correlate with increased monocyte accumulation in the CNS.
source: fWBI-induced cognitive deficits has been shown to correlate with increased monocyte accumulation in the CNS (Morganti et al., 2014; Moravan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: fWBI induced significant increase of peripherally derived monocytes in the contralateral brain hemisphere to the tumor.
source: fWBI induced significant increase of peripherally derived monocytes in the contralateral brain hemisphere to the tumor (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4B.

claim: Treatment with the CSF-1R inhibitor induced a partial depletion of microglia in both irradiated and non-irradiated mice.
source: Treatment with the CSF-1R inhibitor induced a partial depletion of microglia, in both irradiated and non-irradiated mice (Figure 4A) and prevented radiation-induced infiltration of peripherally derived monocytes (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4A.

claim: CSF-1R inhibitor treatment prevented radiation-induced infiltration of peripherally derived monocytes.
source: Treatment with the CSF-1R inhibitor induced a partial depletion of microglia, in both irradiated and non-irradiated mice (Figure 4A) and prevented radiation-induced infiltration of peripherally derived monocytes (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4B.

claim: The results on myeloid cell changes are in line with previous findings in a tumor-free radiation model.
source: These results are in line with our previous findings in a tumor-free radiation model (Morganti et al., 2014; Feng et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous work by the authors, supported by citations.

claim: In the ipsilateral hemisphere, inflammatory monocyte numbers correlate with the size of tumors.
source: However, in the ipsilateral hemisphere inflammatory monocyte numbers correlate with the size of tumors (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by correlation data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Changes in contralateral myeloid cells are unaffected by the growth of tumors in the ipsilateral brain hemisphere.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that changes in contralateral myeloid cells are unaffected by the growth of tumors in the ipsilateral brain hemisphere.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of ipsilateral and contralateral hemisphere data.

claim: The cell line used for the GL261 model is driven by KRAS and p53, a combination of mutation rarely seen in human glioma patients.
source: It is important to acknowledge that the cell line used for the GL261 model is driven by KRAS and p53, a combination of mutation rarely seen in human glioma patients.
evidence: This reflects knowledge about the genetic characteristics of the GL261 model and human gliomas.

claim: Differences in genetic and molecular features may affect the inflammatory microenvironment of the tumor.
source: These differences in genetic and molecular features may affect the inflammatory microenvironment of the tumor (Mackay et al., 2018), and in turn influence cognitive outcomes measured in this study.
evidence: This is speculation about potential limitations, supported by a citation.

claim: Differences in genetic and molecular features may influence cognitive outcomes measured in this study.
source: These differences in genetic and molecular features may affect the inflammatory microenvironment of the tumor (Mackay et al., 2018), and in turn influence cognitive outcomes measured in this study.
